newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: "Stolen" Aborigines lose High Court case.
newsitem.headline: "Stolen" Aborigines lose High Court case.

text.p: Australia's highest court ruled on Thursday that a group of Aborigines taken from their parents by past Australian governments under an assimilation law could not sue for compensation.

The High Court ruled that no constitutional right existed for the Aborigines to take action against the Australian government because the Northern Territory, which it administers, had acted in accordance with laws in place at the time.
A group of nine Aborigines had sought the right to sue for compensation after they were forcibly taken as children from their families under a Northern Territory assimilation law.
"They have virtually sanctioned the removal of us and our mothers and that to us is just devastating," Barbara Cummings, one of the nine Aborigines, told reporters.
Tens of thouands of Aboriginal children were forcibly removed from their parents under Australian government assimilation laws from the early 1900s to the 1960s.
Australia's human rights body has called the assimilation policy attempted genocide and called on the government to formally apologise.
Prime Minister John Howard has issued a personal apology, but refuses to issue a formal government apology.
The High Court ruling was a landmark finding against hundreds of Aborigines who had been seeking compensation from the Australian government.

The nine were among the first of more than 600 Aborigines from the rugged but resource-rich Northern Territory to seek compensation, while Aborigines in other parts of Australia have also lodged compensation writs.
The dimissed writs had sought that the government accept responsibility for the past policy of forcibly taking Aboriginal children from their families and assimilating them into the white community.

"We are talking about genocide here," said Matthew Storey, a lawyer for the publicly funded Aboriginal Legal Service before the ruling. "Now it would be a shame if genocide wasn't prohibitied by our constitution."
The High Court in Canberra had deliberated for 17 months after hearing evidence in the case in February 1996.
